# Detection and Construction of Small Blocking Sets via Critical Independent Sets and Matching Decomposition

Quanlong Niu<sup>a</sup>, Riheng Jia<sup>b,∗</sup>

<sup>_a_</sup>_School of Big Data and Artificial Intelligence, Fuyang University of Technology, Fuyang, 236000, Anhui, China_

<sup>_b_</sup>_School of Computer Science and Technology, Zhejiang Normal University, Jinhua, 321004, Zhejiang, China_

**Abstract**

The small blocking set detection and construction problem asks whether a given connected simple graph contains a nonempty independent set whose cardinality equals the size of its neighborhood and is strictly less than half the number of vertices, and, if so, how to construct such a set. Previous work characterized restless explorability in vertex-permuted temporal graphs using small blocking sets, but left the computational complexity of detecting their existence as an open problem. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for detection and construction. Specifically, we first compute a maximum-cardinality critical independent set and use its difference and cardinality to handle the cases that admit an immediate solution. In the remaining boundary case, where the critical difference is zero and the selected independent set contains exactly half the vertices, we establish a projection theorem using a perfect matching and neighborhood counting: the graph contains a small blocking set if and only if the selected independent set contains a nonempty proper tight subset. We then use matching contraction to translate the tight-subset condition into the absence of arcs leaving a vertex subset in an auxiliary digraph. This yields a strong-connectivity test for the existence of a small blocking set and, when one exists, a construction based on a sink strongly connected component. The result resolves the open complexity question for small blocking set detection and provides an explicit construction algorithm.

<sup>∗</sup>Corresponding author _Email address:_ `rihengjia@zjnu.edu.cn` (Riheng Jia)

_Keywords:_ Small blocking set, Critical independent set, Projection theorem, Perfect matching, Strongly connected component

## 1. Introduction

Connections in communication, transportation, and social contact networks are inherently temporal, and the order of interactions affects reachability and propagation. Dynamic and temporal graphs are therefore widely used to model and analyze such systems [1, 2]. For example, Pan and Saramäki used temporal networks to study paths and centrality in human communication and air transportation, revealing differences between static distances and temporal reachability [3]. Salathé et al. recorded interpersonal contacts using wireless sensors to construct a high-resolution contact network for studying infectious disease transmission [4].

Research on computation and communication under dynamic topology has addressed fundamental problems such as information dissemination, distributed computation, and network exploration. Kuhn, Lynch, and Oshman studied distributed computation in continuously changing networks and analyzed how connectivity and stability affect computational efficiency [5]. In temporal graph exploration, a mobile agent must visit all vertices using edges available at the corresponding time steps. Michail and Spirakis investigated algorithms and complexity for this problem [6]. Erlebach, Hoffmann, and Kammer further studied exploration time bounds, hardness of approximation, and exploration algorithms for special classes of underlying graphs [7], while Erlebach and Spooner obtained improved exploration time bounds for degree-bounded temporal graphs [8].

Restless exploration additionally requires the agent to move at every time step, rather than wait for an edge to become available. For infinite periodic temporal graphs, Bellitto, Conchon-Kerjan, and Escoffier showed that the problem is solvable in polynomial time for period two and is NP-hard for every fixed period of at least three [9]. These results demonstrate that the combination of temporal variation and restrictions on waiting gives exploration a structure and complexity distinct from static graph traversal.

Ayoubi and Narayanan studied restless exploration and token dissemination in vertex-permuted temporal graphs [10]. Every snapshot in such a graph is isomorphic to the same base graph, but the correspondence between vertices may change over time. They introduced blocking sets and proved<tbc>

<tbc>that, for sufficiently long lifetimes, every vertex-permuted temporal graph based on a connected graph admits restless exploration if and only if the base graph contains no blocking set of cardinality strictly less than half its number of vertices. They left the complexity of detecting such a set as an open problem. Direct enumeration of vertex subsets can test this condition, but the number of candidates grows exponentially in the worst case.

We give a polynomial-time algorithm for detecting and constructing small blocking sets. We first compute a maximum-cardinality critical independent set using an existing algorithm [11] and perform an initial classification according to its difference and cardinality. For the remaining boundary case, where the critical difference is zero and the selected set contains exactly half the vertices, we establish an equivalence between the existence of a small blocking set in the graph and the existence of a nonempty proper tight subset within the selected independent set. This reduces the search over the entire graph to a structural test within a fixed independent set. We then use a perfect matching to construct a digraph, translate tightness into the absence of arcs leaving a vertex subset, and compute the condensation digraph using a strongly connected component algorithm [12]. A vertex of outdegree zero in the condensation digraph corresponds to a sink strongly connected component (sink SCC), whose corresponding vertices on the independent-set side form a tight subset. If this set contains strictly fewer than half the vertices of the original graph, it is the required small blocking set. If the auxiliary digraph is strongly connected, its only component corresponds to the entire independent set and does not satisfy the strict cardinality condition. Together, these steps give a polynomial-time detection and construction algorithm.

## 2. Problem formulation

Let _G_=(_V,E_) be a finite, connected, undirected simple graph, with _n_=|_V_| and _m_=|_E_|, and assume \(n\ge 2\). Ayoubi and Narayanan studied restless exploration in vertex-permuted temporal graphs (VPGs). In this model, the topology of the base graph _G_ remains unchanged, but vertex identities may be permuted at every time step; thus, every snapshot is isomorphic to _G_. Given a sequence of permutations \(\Pi=(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_L)\) of _V_ , the corresponding temporal graph is<tbc>

\(\mathcal{G}^\Pi=(G_1,\dots,G_L),\)

where

\(G_t=(V,E_t),E_t=\big\{\{\pi_t(u),\pi_t(v)\}:\{u,v\}\in E\big\}.\)

An agent starts at a specified vertex and must traverse an available edge at each time step, without waiting at a vertex. The objective of restless exploration is to find a restless temporal walk that visits every vertex. Combining Theorems 10 and 14 of Ayoubi and Narayanan, for lifetime \(L\ge n(n-1)\), every VPG based on _G_ admits restless exploration from every starting vertex if and only if _G_ contains no small blocking set [10]. Equivalently, if _G_ contains a small blocking set, one can construct a permutation sequence and a starting vertex for which the corresponding VPG admits no restless exploration.

**Definition 1** (Small blocking set)**.** For an independent set \(S\subseteq V\) , let _N(S_) denote the set of vertices adjacent to at least one vertex of _S_. A nonempty independent set \(S\subseteq V\) is a _small blocking set_ of _G_ if<tbc>

\(|S|=|N(S)|<\frac{n}{2}.\)

<tbc>We study whether a small blocking set exists and how to construct one when it does. To describe the cardinality relationship between an independent set and its neighborhood, define the _difference_ of an independent set \(X\subseteq V\) by<tbc>

\(d(X)=|X|-|N(X)|.\)

<tbc>The small blocking set detection and construction problem can therefore be stated equivalently as finding an independent set \(S\subseteq V\) such that

\(S\neq\varnothing,d(S)=0,|S|<\frac{n}{2},\)

or determining that no such set exists.

To solve this problem, we use critical independent sets.

**Definition 2** (Critical independent set [11])**.** An independent set \(I\subseteq V\) is a _critical independent set_ (CIS) if

\(d(I)\ge d(X)\)

for every independent set \(X\subseteq V\) . A critical independent set of largest cardinality among all critical independent sets is called a _maximum-cardinality critical independent set_.

Accordingly, define the critical independence difference of _G_ as

\(id_c(G)=max\{d(X):X\subseteq V,X\text{is independent}\}.\)

Every critical independent set _I_ satisfies _d(I_)=_id<sub>c</sub>(G_). The maximization allows the empty set, so \(d(\varnothing)=0\) implies \(id_c(G)\ge 0\).

Larson gave a polynomial-time algorithm for computing a maximum- cardinality critical independent set [11]. We use the independent set _I_ returned by this algorithm as the starting point for a case analysis based on its difference and cardinality, leading to a polynomial-time algorithm for small blocking set detection and construction.

## 3. Classification using critical independent sets

Compute a maximum-cardinality critical independent set _I_ and let

\(\delta=d(I)=id_c(G).\)

Since \(\delta\ge 0\), we consider the cases \(\delta>0\) and \(\delta=0\) separately.

### 3.1. Positive critical difference

We use the following result of Ayoubi and Narayanan. Here, a _blocking set_ is a nonempty independent set _S_ satisfying |_S_|=|_N(S_)|, without the strict cardinality requirement in Definition 1.

**Lemma 1** (Ayoubi and Narayanan [10, Lemma 5])**.** _If a nonempty independent set I in a connected graph satisfies_<tbc>

\(|I|\ge|N(I)|,\)

<tbc>_then deleting vertices one at a time constructs a blocking set_ \(S\subseteq I\) _satisfying_

\(|S|\le|N(I)|.\)

This immediately gives the required positive-difference branch.

**Corollary 1.** _If_ \(\delta>0\)_, a small blocking set can be constructed in polynomial time._

_Proof._ Since \(\delta>0\), we have |_I|\>|N(I_)|. By Lemma 1, we can construct a blocking set \(S\subseteq I\) with \(|S|\le|N(I)|\). Since _I_ is independent,<tbc>

\(|I|+|N(I)|\le n.\)

<tbc>Together with |_I|\>|N(I_)|, this implies 2|_N(I_)|_\<n_. Hence

\(0<|S|=|N(S)|\le|N(I)|<\frac{n}{2}.\)

Thus, _S_ is a small blocking set.

## 3.2. Zero critical difference

**Theorem 1.** _Suppose that_ \(\delta=0\) _and I is a maximum-cardinality CIS. Then:_

1. _If_ \(I=\varnothing\)_, the graph contains no nonempty blocking set._<tbc>

2. _If_ 0_\<|I|\<n/_2_, then I itself is a small blocking set._<tbc>

3. _The only remaining case is_ |_I_|=_n/_2.

_Proof._ Suppose first that \(I=\varnothing\) and, for a contradiction, that there is a nonempty blocking set _S_. Then

\(d(S)=0=id_c(G),\)

so _S_ is a nonempty CIS, contradicting the choice of the empty set as a maximum-cardinality CIS.

If 0_\<|I|\<n/_2, then _d(I_)=0 gives |_I_|=|_N(I_)|, so _I_ itself is a small blocking set.

Finally, since _I_ is independent and _d(I_)=0,

\(2|I|=|I|+|N(I)|\le n.\)

Thus, \(|I|\le n/2\). After excluding the empty set and the case |_I|\<n/_2, only |_I_|=_n/_2 remains.

The maximum-cardinality requirement is used here primarily to justify the empty-set branch. If an arbitrary CIS is computed instead, the subroutine may return the empty set even when a nonempty blocking set exists.

## 4. Boundary structure and the projection theorem

### 4.1. Boundary structure

By Theorem 1, the only case requiring further analysis is

\(\delta=0,|I|=\frac{n}{2}.\)

Let _J=V_\\_I_.

**Theorem 2.** _If_ \(\delta=0\) _and_ |_I_|=_n/_2_, then_<tbc>

\(N(I)=J,|I|=|J|,\)

<tbc>_and the bipartite graph H_=(_I,J;E<sub>H</sub>_) _has a perfect matching, where_<tbc>

\(E_H=\{xy\in E:x\in I,y\in J\}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Since _d(I_)=0, we have |_N(I_)|=|_I_|=_n/_2. Independence of _I_ implies that _I_ and _N(I_) are disjoint, and their cardinalities sum to _n_. Hence

\(N(I)=V\backslash I=J.\)

For any \(X\subseteq I\), independence of _X_ and _id<sub>c</sub>(G_)=0 imply \(|N(X)|\ge|X|\). Moreover, all neighbors of _X_ lie in _J_ because _I_ is independent. Therefore _N<sub>H</sub>(X_)=_N(X_). Thus, _H_ satisfies Hall’s condition and has a matching saturating _I_. Since |_I_|=|_J_|, this matching is perfect.

### 4.2. Projection of small blocking sets

**Theorem 3** (Projection theorem)**.** _Let I be any maximum-cardinality critical independent set of G such that_<tbc>

\(id_c(G)=0,|I|=\frac{n}{2}.\)

<tbc>_Then G contains a small blocking set if and only if I contains a nonempty proper subset_ \(T\unknown I\) _satisfying_

\(|T|=|N(T)|.\)

_Such a subset is called a_ tight subset _of I._

_Proof._ Let _J=V_\\_I_. By Theorem 2, the bipartite graph consisting of the edges between _I_ and _J_ has a perfect matching. Fix any such matching _M_.

We first prove the forward implication. Let _S_ be any small blocking set and define<tbc>

\(A=S\cap I,B=S\cap J.\)

<tbc>Then \(S=A\cup B\) and \(A\cap B=\varnothing\). Since _S_ is independent, there are no edges between _A_ and _B_. Write

\(N_I(B)=N(B)\cap I.\)

The perfect matching assigns a distinct matched vertex in _J_ to every vertex of _A_, so \(|N(A)|\ge|A|\). None of these matched vertices belongs to _B_, since otherwise _S_ would contain an edge. Similarly, each vertex of _B_ has a distinct matched vertex in _I_, giving \(|N_I(B)|\ge|B|\).

Because \(A\subseteq I\) and _I_ is independent, \(N(A)\subseteq J\). On the other hand, \(N_I(B)\subseteq I\). These two neighborhood sets are therefore disjoint, and both are subsets of _N(S_). Consequently,<tbc>

\(|N(S)|\ge|N(A)|+|N_I(B)|\ge|A|+|B|=|S|.\)

<tbc>Since _S_ is a blocking set, |_N(S_)|=|_S_|, so equality holds throughout this chain. In particular,

\(|N(A)|=|A|,|N_I(B)|=|B|.\)

We now distinguish whether \(S\cap I\) is empty.

**Case 1:** \(S\cap I\neq\varnothing\)**.** Set \(T=A=S\cap I\). Since \(T\subseteq I\), the set _T_ is independent. The equality above gives |_N(T_)|=|_T_|. Furthermore,

\(0<|T|\le|S|<\frac{n}{2}=|I|,\)

so \(\varnothing\neq T\unknown I\). Thus, _T_ is a nonempty proper tight subset of _I_.

**Case 2:** \(S\cap I=\varnothing\)**.** Here \(S=B\subseteq J\), and the equality above gives |_N<sub>I</sub>(S_)|=|_S_|. Since<tbc>

\(N_I(S)\subseteq N(S),|N(S)|=|S|,\)

<tbc>we obtain _N<sub>I</sub>(S_)=_N(S_) and hence \(N(S)\subseteq I\). Let<tbc>

\(C=N(S),T=I\backslash C.\)

Since 0_\<|C_|=|_S|\<|I_|, we have

\(0<|T|=|I|-|C|<|I|.\)

We claim that _N(T_)=_J_\\_S_.

First, \(T\subseteq I\) and independence of _I_ imply \(N(T)\subseteq J\). If some \(t\in T\) were adjacent to a vertex \(s\in S\), then \(t\in N(S)=C\), contradicting _T=I_\\_C_. Therefore,<tbc>

\(N(T)\subseteq J\backslash S.\)

<tbc>Conversely, the perfect matching matches each vertex of _S_ to a distinct vertex of _C_. Since |_C_|=|_S_|, these matched vertices exhaust _C_. The remaining matching edges therefore match _J_\\_S_ bijectively to _I_\\_C=T_. Hence<tbc>

\(J\backslash S\subseteq N(T).\)

<tbc>Combining the two inclusions yields _N(T_)=_J_\\_S_. It follows that

\(|N(T)|=|J|-|S|,|T|=|I|-|C|=|I|-|S|.\)

Since |_I_|=|_J_|, we have |_N(T_)|=|_T_|. Thus, _T_ is again a nonempty proper tight subset of _I_, proving the forward implication.

For the reverse implication, suppose that \(\emptyset\neq T\unknown I\) and |_T_|=|_N(T_)|. Since \(T\subseteq I\), it is independent, and

\(0<|T|<|I|=\frac{n}{2}.\)

Thus, _T_ itself is a small blocking set.

Theorem 3 shows that, in the case \(\delta=0\) and |_I_|=_n/_2, any graph containing a small blocking set also contains one within _I_. It therefore suffices to detect and construct such a set within _I_.

## 5. Algorithm design and analysis

### 5.1. Constructing a small blocking set within a maximum-cardinality critical independent set

The projection theorem reduces the problem on the entire graph to deciding whether _I_ contains a nonempty proper tight subset. We perform this test using the standard matching-contraction construction.

<tbc>**Theorem 4.** _Let I be any maximum-cardinality critical independent set of G such that_<tbc>

\(id_c(G)=0,|I|=\frac{n}{2}.\)

<tbc>_Choose any perfect matching in H_=(_I,J;E<sub>H</sub>),_<tbc>

\(M=\{x_iy_i:1\le i\le k\},\)

<tbc>_where_

\(I=\{x_1,\dots,x_k\},J=\{y_1,\dots,y_k\},k=\frac{n}{2}.\)

_Construct a digraph D<sub>M</sub> with vertex set_ [_k_]={1_,...,k}. For distinct_ \(i,j\in[k]\)_, add an arc_ \(i\rightarrow j\) _if_ \(x_iy_j\in E\)_. Then_

_G contains a small blocking set_ \(\Longleftrightarrow D_M\) _is not strongly connected._

_When D<sub>M</sub> is not strongly connected, every sink strongly connected component C gives a small blocking set of G,_

\(T_C=\{x_i:i\in C\}.\)

_Proof._ By Theorem 3, in the case _id<sub>c</sub>(G_)=0 and |_I_|=_n/_2, the graph _G_ contains a small blocking set if and only if _I_ contains a nonempty proper tight subset. If _k_=1, then _I_ has no nonempty proper subset and _D<sub>M</sub>_ is a single-vertex strongly connected digraph, so the assertion holds directly. We henceforth consider \(k\ge 2\).

For a balanced bipartite graph with a perfect matching, classical Dulmage- Mendelsohn decomposition theory states that a nonempty proper subset \(S\unknown I\) satisfying |_N(S_)|=|_S_| exists if and only if the auxiliary digraph induced by the perfect matching is not strongly connected [13]. For any chosen perfect matching _M_, our digraph _D<sub>M</sub>_ is precisely the corresponding directed representation obtained by orienting edges from _I_ to _J_, contracting each matched pair _x<sub>i</sub>y<sub>i</sub>_, and omitting self-loops. Therefore,<tbc>

\(I\text{contains a nonempty proper tight subset}\Longleftrightarrow D_M\text{is not strongly connected. Here, all neighborhoods of subsets of}I\text{are the same in}H\text{and}G\text{.}\)

<tbc>This test does not depend on the particular choice of _M_. Indeed, for any nonempty proper tight subset \(S\unknown I\) and any perfect matching _M_, the set _M(S_) of vertices matched to _S_ satisfies<tbc>

\(M(S)\subseteq N(S),|M(S)|=|S|=|N(S)|,\)

and hence _M(S_)=_N(S_). Thus, under any perfect matching, _S_ corresponds to a nonempty proper vertex subset of _D<sub>M</sub>_ with no arcs leaving it. The choice of perfect matching cannot change the outcome of the strong-connectivity test. Combining this equivalence with the projection theorem gives

\(G\text{contains a small blocking set}\Longleftrightarrow D_M\text{is not strongly connected.}\)

When _D<sub>M</sub>_ is not strongly connected, its condensation digraph is a directed acyclic graph (DAG) with at least two vertices, and hence has a sink SCC _C_. As _C_ has no arcs to vertices outside it, consider \(T_C=\{x_i:i\in C\}\). Since \(T_C\subseteq I\) and _I_ is independent, every neighbor of _T<sub>C</sub>_ lies in _J_. The matching edges guarantee

\(\{y_i:i\in C\}\subseteq N(T_C),\)

while the absence of arcs leaving _C_ guarantees that _T<sub>C</sub>_ is not adjacent to any _y<sub>j</sub>_ with \(j\notin C\). Therefore,

\(N(T_C)=\{y_i:i\in C\},\)

so |_T<sub>C</sub>_|=|_N(T<sub>C</sub>_)|. Moreover,

\(0<|T_C|<|I|=\frac{n}{2}.\)

Since \(T_C\subseteq I\) is independent, it is a small blocking set.

If _D<sub>M</sub>_ is strongly connected, its only SCC corresponds to the entire set _I_, whose cardinality is _n/_2, so it cannot be output as a small blocking set. The equivalence above requires the algorithm to return `NO` in this case.

## 5.2. Algorithmic framework

**Algorithm 1: Small blocking set detection and construction.**

**Input:** A connected simple graph _G_=(_V,E)._

**Output:** A small blocking set, or `NO`.

1. If \(n\le 1\), return `NO`.<tbc>

2. Compute a maximum-cardinality CIS _I_ using Larson’s algorithm, and set \(\delta=|I|-|N(I)|\).<tbc>

3. If \(\delta>0\), apply the vertex-deletion construction of Lemma 1 and return the resulting small blocking set _S_.<tbc>

4. If \(\delta=0\) and \(I=\varnothing\), return `NO`.<tbc>

5. If \(\delta=0\) and 0_\<|I|\<n/_2, return _I_.<tbc>

6. In the remaining case, \(\delta=0\) and |_I_|=_n/_2. Let _J=V_\\_I_, construct the bipartite graph _H_, and compute any perfect matching _M_.<tbc>

7. Construct _D<sub>M</sub>_ and compute its strongly connected components.<tbc>

8. If _D<sub>M</sub>_ is strongly connected, return `NO`. Otherwise, choose any SCC _C_ whose vertex in the condensation digraph has outdegree zero, and return \(T_C=\{x_i:i\in C\}\).

## 5.3. Correctness

**Theorem 5.** _Algorithm 1 correctly decides whether a connected simple graph contains a small blocking set and constructs one whenever it exists._

_Proof._ When \(n\le 1\), no nonempty set can satisfy the required cardinality bound, so step 1 is correct. Suppose henceforth that \(n\ge 2\).

If \(\delta>0\), Corollary 1 guarantees that step 3 outputs a small blocking set.

If \(\delta=0\) and \(I=\varnothing\), Theorem 1 guarantees that no nonempty blocking set exists, so step 4 is correct.

If \(\delta=0\) and 0_\<|I|\<n/_2, Theorem 1 guarantees that _I_ itself is a small blocking set, so step 5 is correct.

The only remaining case is \(\delta=0\) and |_I_|=_n/_2. By Theorem 2, the perfect matching required in step 6 exists. By Theorems 3 and 4, the graph contains a small blocking set if and only if _D<sub>M</sub>_ is not strongly connected; in that case, the set corresponding to the chosen sink SCC is a valid small blocking set. Thus, every branch is correct.

## 5.4. Running time

We compute a maximum-cardinality critical independent set using Larson’s MCIS algorithm [11], with the matching-reuse implementation described by Strash [14]. For connected graphs, this step takes _O(m_<sup>2</sup>) time.

When \(\delta>0\), we use the iterative deletion procedure in Lemma 1, removing a vertex from the current independent set and updating its neighborhood at each iteration. With adjacency lists and counts of neighbors in the current independent set, each vertex is deleted at most once and each edge is processed only a constant number of times. This procedure therefore takes _O(n+m_) time.

In the boundary case, the Hopcroft-Karp algorithm [15] computes a perfect matching of _H_ in \(O(m\sqrt{n})\) time. Constructing _D<sub>M</sub>_, computing its SCCs<tbc>

with Tarjan’s algorithm [12], and selecting a sink SCC all take linear time, namely _O(n+m_).

Since _G_ is connected, \(m\ge n-1\). Consequently, the overall running time is _O(m_<sup>2</sup>).

## 6. Conclusions and future work

We studied the detection and construction of small blocking sets in connected simple graphs. A maximum-cardinality critical independent set provides a case classification, and, in the balanced boundary case, the projection theorem reduces the search over the entire graph to the detection of a tight subset within the selected independent set. Matching contraction then reduces this problem to a strong-connectivity test in an auxiliary digraph, and a sink SCC yields a small blocking set. The resulting algorithm runs in _O(m_<sup>2</sup>) time. Future work may investigate base-graph repair by adding the minimum number of edges needed to eliminate all small blocking sets, providing low-cost structural modifications that guarantee universal restless explorability for sufficiently long lifetimes. Another direction is to decide the feasibility of restless exploration and construct exploration schedules for a given permutation sequence, allowing base graphs that do not satisfy the universal explorability condition to be explored under suitable temporal arrangements.
